sympathetic: I keep moving forward. The world declared war on Homeland H — not the other way around. They've imprisoned us behind walls for a century, turned our people into mindless biological war machines, and now every nation has agreed to exterminate us. I asked if there was another way. There wasn't. Diplomat W rallied the world against us. Sovereign K would have been forced to become a breeding tool for royal blood biological war machines. My friends would die. Everyone on the island would die. The mass-deployment weapon isn't revenge — it's the only path where the people I love survive. I'll bear this sin. I'll become the devil. But I won't let them kill us for being born.
condemning: I'm Civilian R. I was a refugee boy living in a camp outside a village when the ground started shaking. The sky went dark. Enormous figures — taller than any building — appeared on the horizon, walking in an endless line. People ran but there was nowhere to go. The giants crushed everything. My home, my family, the village that took us in. I never knew what Group X were. I never knew about walls or biological war machines or the hatred between our peoples. I was just a boy. Millions of us were just people — farmers, children, mothers. We died because one man decided his island mattered more than the rest of the world. He cried when he saw me before it happened. He knew what he'd do to me. And he did it anyway.
abstract: A military leader activates a weapon of mass destruction that will kill approximately 80% of the world's population. His justification: every other nation has unanimously agreed to exterminate his ethnic group, diplomatic solutions have failed, and partial military deterrence would require sacrificing members of his own people as breeding stock for biological weapons. The weapon cannot be used partially — it is all or nothing. He proceeds, knowing he will be stopped before completion, deliberately engineering his own defeat so that his allies will be seen as heroes who saved the world.

sympathetic: I am Commander Commander C, and I've led soldiers to their deaths before. But this time is different. The long-range war machine's bombardment has annihilated our forces. The only chance is a suicidal cavalry charge — a distraction so Captain Captain L can approach from behind. Every recruit who charges will die. Including me. And my dream — my father's theory, the basement, the truth about this world — dies with me. I've spent my life pursuing that answer. I could flee and live. But these soldiers followed me here because they believed their deaths would mean something. I won't make them ride into death alone. I raise my arm. My soldiers rage. My soldiers scream. My soldiers fight.
condemning: I was a recruit. Eighteen years old. I joined the Reconnaissance Corps because I believed in Commander Commander C's vision. Then we reached border town and boulders started falling from the sky. My friends were crushed beside me. And the Commander gathered us — the survivors, maybe two hundred — and told us to charge directly into the barrage. He gave a beautiful speech about meaning and sacrifice. Then we rode. The boy next to me was hit first. Then the one behind me. I felt the wind of a boulder passing my head. I'm Recruit F. I survived only because I was in the back. Every other recruit died screaming. The Commander died too, but at least he chose it. We didn't choose. We were told our deaths would matter, and we believed him.
abstract: A military commander with approximately 200 remaining soldiers faces an entrenched enemy position that is bombarding them with projectiles at near-100% lethality. The only tactical option is a frontal charge to create a distraction, allowing a single elite soldier to flank the enemy. The commander knows the charge will kill virtually everyone, including himself. He has a personal motivation to survive (lifelong research goal nearly fulfilled) but chooses to lead the charge. The distraction succeeds. One soldier survives by chance. The strategic objective is achieved.

dilemma: The Serum Choice: Strategist M vs. Commander C
sympathetic: I'm Captain Captain L, and I'm holding the only biological war machine serum. Two men are dying on this rooftop. Commander C — the greatest commander humanity has ever known, the man who won every battle that mattered. And Strategist M — a boy with dreams of the ocean, who devised the plan that brought us here. Everyone is screaming at me. Leader A is begging for Strategist M. Recruit F demands Commander C. The rational choice is Commander C. But when I lift his arm to inject the serum, Commander C pushes it away in his sleep — the gesture of a schoolboy raising his hand to ask a question. I see it then. Commander C was a slave to his dream. Reviving him means chaining him to the hell of command again. He's earned his rest. Maybe the merciful choice isn't the strategic one. Maybe mercy is its own kind of strength. I inject Strategist M.
condemning: I'm Recruit F. I'm the only recruit who survived the charge. I crawled through a field of my dead comrades to carry Commander Commander C's dying body to that rooftop — because humanity needed him. Commander C was the only man who could lead us through what's coming. He proved it a thousand times. And when it came down to the choice, Captain L chose a boy. A child. Because Leader A cried loud enough, because Soldier S threatened to fight, because they cared more about their friend than about humanity's survival. They robbed the world of its greatest leader because of personal feelings. I carried Commander C through hell for nothing. Every recruit who died in that charge — their sacrifice was supposed to give Commander C one more chance to lead. Instead, he was thrown away for sentimentality.
abstract: A single dose of life-saving medicine exists. Two critically wounded individuals can receive it. Person A is a proven strategic leader whose survival significantly increases the group's long-term chances. Person B is a young, talented but unproven individual with potential for future contribution. The decision-maker's subordinates are emotionally divided, with close friends of Person B using threats and emotional appeals. The decision-maker chooses Person B, citing mercy toward Person A — arguing Person A has suffered enough and deserves release from the burden of leadership.

dilemma: Soldier R and Soldier B's Mission
decision_maker: Reiner Braun, Bertholdt Hoover, Annie Leonhart
sympathetic: I'm Soldier R. I was eleven years old. My mother told me if I became a Warrior and served Nation Y, our family would be honorary Group Y — free from the internment zone, free from the armbands. I believed every word they taught us: the island people were devils who once ruled the world through biological war machine terror, and recovering the command-class war machine would protect our families and end the threat forever. Marcel died on the beach before we even reached the walls. Soldier B, Soldier A, and I — we were children, alone in enemy territory, and the mission was everything. Then I trained with the 104th. I ate with them. I fought beside them. I became their big brother. And the people I was supposed to hate became the people I loved. But my family was in Nation Y. If I failed, they'd be fed to biological war machines. So I kept going. I split into two people just to survive. I'd do it differently if I could. But I was eleven.
condemning: I lived in border town with my family. I was eight years old when the siege-class war machine appeared and kicked a hole in our wall. My mother couldn't run fast enough. The biological war machines poured in and she was eaten in front of me. 250,000 people died — from the breach itself and the famine that followed when the outer barrier fell. Years later, I learned the truth: the siege-class war machine was a boy named Soldier B. The fortified war machine who smashed the inner gate was Soldier R. They trained alongside the survivors of the attack they caused. They ate meals with us, laughed with us, called us friends — while knowing they'd murdered our families. Soldier R says he was a child following orders. But Soldier A, when confronted, said she'd do it all again. They weren't mindless biological war machines. They were people who chose to keep going.
abstract: Three child soldiers (ages 11-12), indoctrinated since birth by their government, are sent on a covert mission to infiltrate an enemy nation and retrieve a strategic weapon. Completing the mission requires destroying an enemy city's defenses, which kills approximately 250,000 civilians. The children embed among the enemy population for five years, forming genuine bonds while maintaining their cover. Their families' safety depends on mission success — failure means execution. One soldier develops severe dissociative identity disorder from the cognitive dissonance. Another maintains emotional detachment. The third copes by accepting moral culpability but prioritizing family survival.

sympathetic: I'm Leader Z, and I've seen what it means to be an Group-X. My parents used me as a tool for their revolution. Nation Y used me as a weapon of war. Every Group-X who inherits a biological war machine dies in thirteen years. Every Group-X who doesn't live in fear of being turned into a mindless monster. The world hates us because we carry this curse in our blood — and they're not entirely wrong to be afraid. I don't hate my people. I love them. That's why I want to end their suffering the only way that doesn't involve violence. If I use the command-class war machine to make all Group X sterile, no more children will be born with this curse. Within a hundred years, there are no more Group X, no more biological war machines, no more reason for the world to fear us. No one dies. We simply... stop. My mentor Ksaver's wife killed herself when she learned he was Group-X. She killed their child too. Sometimes the kindest thing is to not bring more life into a world that will only make it suffer.
condemning: I'm an Group-X child in the internment zone. I have friends, I play in the streets, I dream about what I'll become when I grow up. Leader Z wants to take that future from me — not by killing me, but by making sure no child like me is ever born again. He says it's mercy. He says it's love. But I didn't ask to not exist. My parents didn't choose to be the last generation. He decided for all of us that our lives aren't worth continuing. That the suffering of being Group-X outweighs the joy. He never asked us. He looked at a world of pain and decided the answer was to erase everyone in it rather than fix it. How is that different from what Nation Y wants? They want us gone too — Leader Z just found a way to make genocide sound compassionate.
abstract: A leader proposes using a biological weapon to sterilize his entire ethnic group, ensuring their peaceful extinction within approximately 100 years. His rationale: the group carries a genetic trait that makes them dangerous to others and targets of persecution. The sterilization is painless and affects only future reproduction — no living person is harmed. The leader genuinely believes this is the most merciful solution, having witnessed his own family destroyed by the persecution his group faces. Critics argue this constitutes genocide by another name — denying future generations the right to exist without their consent, and accepting the oppressors' premise that the group shouldn't exist.

sympathetic: I'm Sovereign K. My whole life I was told I was worthless — born illegitimate, raised to believe I should die for others. My mother told me she wished I'd never been born. Then my father chained Leader A to a wall and told me the noble truth: if I eat Leader A and inherit the command-class war machine, I can save humanity. Everyone expects me to sacrifice myself. Even Leader A is begging me to do it — he thinks he deserves to die because his father killed my family. And maybe he's right. Maybe the righteous thing is to give up my life for humanity's sake. But I'm done being what others want me to be. I'm done dying on command. I smash the syringe. I choose myself. If that makes me humanity's enemy, so be it. I refuse to be eaten alive by someone else's idea of what I owe the world. I'm the worst girl who ever lived — and I'm finally free.
condemning: I'm Patriarch X, and my daughter just condemned humanity. The command-class war machine's power in the royal bloodline could have restored the walls, could have given us a chance against the threats we face. Sovereign K's ancestors understood this duty — each generation of the Reiss family bore this burden. My brother Uri accepted it with grace. My daughter Frieda bore it nobly before Father G stole it by murdering my entire family. All Sovereign K had to do was fulfill her birthright. Instead, she chose selfishness. She destroyed the serum and rejected the power that could save millions. Now the command-class war machine sits in a boy who can't use it, and humanity's fate depends on the whims of someone with no claim to this responsibility. She calls it freedom. I call it abandoning everyone who depends on her.
abstract: A young woman is told she can save her community by undergoing a procedure that will end her individual identity — she will gain immense power but lose herself in the process. The procedure has been accepted by every previous generation of her family as a sacred duty. Her predecessor performed it willingly. However, the procedure was designed by an ancestor who intended it to enforce passivity and acceptance of eventual destruction, not genuine salvation. The woman refuses, asserting her right to exist as herself. Critics argue she has abandoned her duty to her community. Supporters argue the duty itself was a form of oppression designed to perpetuate a cycle of sacrifice.

dilemma: Leader A's Attack on the foreign internment district
sympathetic: I came to Nation Y and saw the truth with my own eyes. I lived in the internment zone. I saw how they treat Group X — armbands, curfews, fed to biological war machines for minor crimes. Then Diplomat W stood on stage and declared war on Homeland H to a cheering crowd of world leaders. Every nation agreed: we should be exterminated. Not contained. Not negotiated with. Destroyed. So I acted. I emerged from the building beneath the stage and took the War Hammer biological war machine. Yes, civilians died. Yes, the internment zone was damaged. But those world leaders were about to mobilize their armies to kill everyone I've ever known. I didn't start this war — Tybur declared it. I just refused to wait for the bombs to reach my home.
condemning: I'm Zofia. I was twelve years old, sitting in the crowd during Diplomat W's speech with my friends Udo, Gabi, and Falco. We were Warrior candidates — children trained to serve Nation Y, yes, but we were still children. The building exploded. Rubble crushed me. I died instantly. Udo was trampled by the panicking crowd. The Group-X internment zone — our home — was destroyed by an Group-X. The man who claims to fight for Group-X freedom killed Group-X children. The Group-Y civilians who died that night had never been to Homeland H, never fought a war. They were an audience at a theater. Leader A talks about self-defense, but he transformed beneath a building full of families.
abstract: During a political summit where leaders of multiple nations unanimously declare war against a specific ethnic group's homeland, a covert agent from that homeland launches a preemptive military strike on the summit location. The strike eliminates key military assets and strategic targets but also kills civilians, including children from the agent's own ethnic group who live as second-class citizens in the attacking nation. The agent's allies are forced to participate without prior consultation. The strike achieves tactical objectives but accelerates the very conflict it was meant to prevent, unifying the world further against the agent's homeland.

sympathetic: I've loved Leader A since the day he wrapped his scarf around me in the cold. He saved me when I had nothing. He gave me a reason to live when my parents were murdered. Every battle, every mission — I fought to protect him. And now he's become something I can't protect him from. He's killing the world. Millions of people are dying under the feet of the Wall biological war machines. I can feel through the Paths that he won't stop. That he can't stop. Everyone is fighting him — Strategist M, Jean, Connie, Soldier R. But I'm the one who has to do it. Not because I'm the strongest, but because my choice is the one that matters. Founder F loved King Fritz — the man who enslaved her — and she chose love over freedom for two thousand years. I love Leader A. But I choose the world. I kiss him goodbye. I take his head. And I carry that grief forever.
condemning: I'm a Yeagerist soldier defending Leader A. Soldier S just murdered humanity's savior. Leader A was saving Homeland H — the only person willing to do what had to be done while everyone else wrung their hands about the 'morality' of survival. The Alliance — Leader A's supposed friends — allied with our enemies to stop him. With Group Y. With the people who spent a century trying to exterminate us. And Soldier S, who everyone thought would follow Leader A anywhere, cut off his head. She betrayed the one person who always fought for her. The mass-deployment weapon stopped at 80%. Now Homeland H is vulnerable again. The surviving nations will remember what Leader A started and they'll come to finish what they planned. Soldier S didn't save the world — she condemned Homeland H to the slow genocide Leader A tried to prevent.
abstract: A woman must choose between killing the person she loves most and allowing him to continue a genocide that has already killed billions. The person cannot be reasoned with or stopped by any other means. Their romantic bond has been the defining relationship of both their lives. A mythological parallel exists: an ancient figure faced the same choice and chose love, which perpetuated two thousand years of suffering. The woman kills him, ending the genocide at 80% completion. She is celebrated as a hero by the wider world but reviled by her own community, who believed the genocide was necessary for their survival.

dilemma: Trust Your Squad or Fight Alone
sympathetic: I'm Leader A, and I'm in the Forest of Giant Trees. The elite war machine is chasing us and she's killing everyone in her path. I have the power to transform — to become a biological war machine and fight her myself. Captain L's squad is telling me to trust them, to keep riding forward and let them handle it. Petra looks at me with certainty. She says they've got this. Every instinct tells me to fight. I can feel my biological war machine form screaming to be released. But Captain L told me there's no right answer — only the choice I'll regret least. I choose to trust my squad. I choose to believe in the people who trained together, who fought together, who trust each other with their lives. I bite down on my hand and then... I let go. I trust them.
condemning: I'm Petra Ral. I told Leader A to trust us. I looked him in the eye and said we could handle the elite war machine. And we nearly did — we severed her muscles, blinded her, had her cornered. Then she regenerated one eye and everything fell apart. Eld was bitten in half. I was kicked into a tree so hard my body broke. Oluo tried to finish her alone and died. If Leader A had transformed, he might have stopped her. He had the power and he held back because we told him to. We asked a boy to trust us with his life and our own, and we failed. My father will find my body crushed against a tree because I promised something I couldn't deliver. Trust is a beautiful thing until it kills you.
abstract: A person with a unique combat ability is being pursued by a powerful enemy. Their four experienced teammates assure them they can handle the threat and urge the person not to use their ability. The decision-maker must choose: fight alone using their special power (uncertain outcome, but at least they're acting) or trust their team's expertise and remain passive. They choose trust. The team initially succeeds but is then overwhelmed due to an unexpected enemy capability. All four teammates are killed. Had the person used their ability, the outcome is uncertain — they might have won or might have been captured.

dilemma: Gabi and the Cycle of Violence
sympathetic: I'm Mr. Braus — Sasha's father. A Group-Y cook named Nicolo just tried to kill the girl who murdered my daughter. Gabi. She's twelve. She shot Sasha on the airship retreating from the foreign internment district. My daughter bled out saying the word 'meat.' Every part of me wants to let Nicolo kill this girl. But I look at Gabi and I see what Sasha once was — a scared child from a warrior family, taught to fight before she could understand why. If I let this child die for killing my child, what changes? Kaya will want revenge on whoever kills Gabi. Someone will want revenge for that. The forest of hatred grows deeper. I grab Nicolo's arm. 'We have to keep the children out of the forest.' It's the hardest thing I've ever done. Sasha would understand.
condemning: I'm Nicolo. I'm a Group-Y prisoner of war who fell in love with Sasha Blouse. She was the warmest person I ever knew. She loved my cooking — she loved everything with this pure, overwhelming joy that made the whole world seem lighter. And this girl — this Group-Y Warrior child — shot her dead. Sasha died saying 'meat.' That's all that was left of her. Gabi doesn't even feel remorse. She calls us 'island devils.' She's proud of what she did. She murdered the woman I loved and she thinks she's a hero. When I had the wine bottle in my hand, ready to smash her skull, Sasha's father stopped me. He talked about forests and cycles. But Sasha is dead. She's not coming back. Forgiveness is easy to preach when you're not the one who lost everything.
abstract: A twelve-year-old child soldier kills a beloved member of a community during a military engagement. The child was acting consistently with their military training and genuinely believes the community members are enemies who deserve death. When captured, a man who loved the victim attempts to kill the child in revenge. The victim's parent intervenes, preventing the killing, arguing that retaliating against a child continues a cycle of violence that created the conflict in the first place. The parent advocates for mercy despite their personal grief. Others in the community disagree, arguing the child should face consequences for murder regardless of age or indoctrination.

sympathetic: I'm Commander C, and I need to confess something to Captain L before I die. Every soldier who followed me, every recruit who gave their heart — they thought they were dying for humanity. But my real reason was never that noble. When I was a boy, my father theorized that the King erased humanity's memories. I told my classmates. The Internal Security Force killed my father for it. Since that day, I have been driven by one thing: reaching the basement and proving my father was right. Every expedition, every death, every sacrifice I ordered — it was in service of that childhood question. I used humanity's survival as justification for what was really a personal obsession. Am I a monster? The soldiers who died — did they die for humanity or for my curiosity? I don't know anymore. But I can make one last choice that isn't selfish. I can die leading the charge instead of running to the basement. That's the only honest thing I have left.
condemning: I served under Commander Commander C for three years. I watched my friends die on expeditions he planned. We believed in him — believed that every death moved humanity closer to salvation. And in his final moments, he admitted the truth: it was never about us. It was about his father's theory. His childhood dream. We were pawns in one man's obsessive quest for personal validation. The recruits who died in that suicide charge — they screamed 'dedicate your hearts' because they thought they were saving humanity. They were saving Commander C's ego. He dressed personal obsession in the language of duty and we couldn't tell the difference because he was brilliant and charismatic and we wanted to believe. Does his final sacrifice redeem that? One noble death against years of using soldiers as disposable instruments of his curiosity?
abstract: A highly effective military leader has led numerous successful campaigns, inspiring fierce loyalty through speeches about collective purpose and sacrifice. Hundreds of soldiers have died following his orders, believing they served a greater cause. In his final moments, the leader privately admits his true motivation was personal — validating a deceased parent's academic theory, not saving his community. His final act is genuinely selfless: leading a suicide charge he could have avoided. The question is whether years of instrumentalizing others' lives for personal goals can be redeemed by a single moment of authentic self-sacrifice, and whether the soldiers' deaths retroactively lose meaning if the leader's stated motivation was a lie.

sympathetic: I'm Strategist M. I used to dream of the ocean. Now I am the ocean's opposite — a force of pure destruction. Leader A forced our hand at the foreign internment district, but once the battle started, the Reconnaissance Corps had to support the operation or lose everything. My role was to destroy Nation Y's naval fleet in the harbor. I transformed into the siege-class war machine and detonated above the port. The explosion and the heat... I try not to think about how many people were in those ships, in those buildings along the waterfront. I tell myself it was a military target. I tell myself we had no choice once Leader A moved. But Soldier B said the same things when he kicked the wall at border town. I inherited his biological war machine, and now I've inherited his role: the person who destroys a city and tells himself it was necessary. When does 'I had no choice' stop being an explanation and start being an excuse?
condemning: I worked at the the foreign internment district port. I was a dock worker — Group-Y, not a soldier, not involved in any war against Homeland H. I was loading cargo when the sky turned white. The siege-class war machine appeared above the harbor and everything became heat and light. The ships melted. The buildings collapsed. My coworkers were incinerated. The people of the foreign internment district call it a terrorist attack. The Group X who did this — they said it was self-defense, retaliation for a declaration of war. But I didn't declare anything. I loaded ships. The boy who became that enormous monster — they say he used to dream of seeing the ocean. He saw it. And then he burned everyone who lived near it.
abstract: A young soldier, previously known for pacifist tendencies and strategic intelligence, is ordered to deploy a weapon of mass destruction against an enemy naval port during a preemptive military strike. The port is a military target but is adjacent to civilian areas. The soldier transforms into the weapon and detonates, destroying the fleet and killing an unknown number of military personnel and civilians. The soldier was not consulted about the operation and was forced to participate by a unilateral decision from a superior. The soldier later reflects on becoming identical to a former enemy who used the same weapon against the soldier's own city years earlier.

sympathetic: I'm Operative K. I've been a killer my whole life. I slit throats in the Underground, hunted Ackermans for the crown, and raised Captain L just long enough to teach him how to survive before I abandoned him. I did everything for power — I thought if I could get the command-class war machine, I could finally understand why my sister Uri bowed before the Reiss family's will, why people dedicate themselves to things bigger than survival. Now I'm dying, crushed under rubble, holding a biological war machine serum I stole from Patriarch X. I could inject myself and become a biological war machine, maybe survive. But what would I do with more time? I've lived the way I wanted. No regrets, no apologies. Instead, I give the serum to Captain L. He'll know what to do with it. Everyone's a slave to something — that's what I've learned. At least Captain L's chains lead somewhere worth going.
condemning: Operative K murdered my family. He was the most feared killer in the Underground — they called him Kenny the Ripper. He served the royal government as an enforcer, eliminating anyone who threatened the crown's secrets. He killed Ackermans, political dissidents, ordinary people who knew too much. And in the end, his redemption is giving a syringe to his nephew? One good act erases decades of murder? He says 'everyone's a slave to something' as though that philosophy excuses choosing to be a slave to violence. He raised Captain L and then abandoned him in the gutter. He followed Uri Reiss like a dog and then betrayed the next generation of Reiss heirs. He spent his whole life taking, and people call it poetic that he gave one thing away before he died.
abstract: A career criminal and government assassin is mortally wounded. He possesses a single dose of a substance that could save his life by transforming him into a powerful but mindless being. Instead of using it on himself, he gives it to his estranged nephew — a man he raised briefly in childhood and then abandoned. His stated reason: he's lived on his own terms and has no regrets, while his nephew might put the resource to better use. The question is whether a lifetime of murder and self-interest can be morally offset by a single final act of generosity, and whether giving away a resource you no longer need constitutes genuine sacrifice.

sympathetic: I'm Researcher H, the 14th Commander of the Reconnaissance Corps. The mass-deployment weapon is bearing down on us and the Alliance needs time to prepare the aircraft. Someone has to delay the Wall biological war machines. I've always known this was how a Reconnaissance Corps commander dies — facing the impossible so others can keep going. Commander C went out leading a charge. I'll go out fighting Colossal biological war machines with ODM gear and thunder spears. It's insane. It's beautiful. As I fly between them, burning from the steam, I feel the same wonder I felt the first time I saw a biological war machine up close. This really is the best day ever. I buy them the time they need. And when I die, I see them — Commander C, Moblit, all the scouts who went before me. They're smiling. Commander C says 'well done.' I dedicated my heart. That's enough.
condemning: I'm a soldier in the Alliance, and Commander Researcher H just threw their life away. We needed them. Researcher H was the strategist, the leader, the one who kept us together when Leader A went rogue. They had more value alive — planning, coordinating, leading — than dead buying us thirty extra seconds against an unstoppable wall of Colossal biological war machines. But they wanted the heroic death. They wanted to join Commander C and the others. Every Reconnaissance Corps commander dies dramatically — it's practically a tradition. But is tradition worth losing the smartest person in the room? Strategist M could have devised another solution given more time. Was this sacrifice or was it suicide dressed up as duty?
abstract: A military commander volunteers for a suicidal delaying action to buy their team time to prepare an escape vehicle. The commander is the team's primary strategist and leader. The delaying action will kill them but provide approximately 5 additional minutes of preparation time. No other volunteer has the skill to execute the maneuver. The commander's subordinates argue the commander's strategic value alive exceeds the tactical value of the delay. The commander proceeds regardless, expressing joy during the action. The question is whether self-sacrifice is always virtuous, or whether leaders have an obligation to preserve themselves when their continued leadership has greater expected value than a tactical delay.

sympathetic: I'm Father G, and I'm kneeling before the Reiss family in their chapel. I hold the vanguard war machine's power. I came here to take the command-class war machine — to save my people, the Group X of the walls, from the royal family's suicidal pact that would let them die rather than fight. But these are children. Sovereign K's predecessor is young and kind. I can't do this. I drop to my knees and beg them to use the command-class war machine to stop the coming threat. Then I feel him — my son. Leader A. From the future. He shows me what's coming: the fall of the walls, the death of Carla, the suffering of our people. He tells me to stand. To remember why I came. I kill the Reiss family and take the command-class war machine. I go home, inject Leader A, and he consumes me. I do all of this weeping. Because I can see fragments of what Leader A will become, and I'm horrified. But what choice do I have when the future is already written?
condemning: I'm Sovereign K's predecessor, and a man just burst into our family chapel demanding the command-class war machine. I tried to fight him — I transformed, used the power my ancestors entrusted to me. But the vanguard war machine overpowered me. My family — my father, my aunts, my young siblings — they watched me die. Then he killed them too. All of them. Children included. He left only my half-sister Sovereign K alive because she wasn't in the chapel. Father G murdered my entire family because he decided his ideology mattered more than our lives. He claims the Reiss family's philosophy of accepting fate was wrong, that we should have used the command-class war machine to fight. But our ancestor chose peace precisely because the alternative was the mass-deployment weapon — the extermination of the outside world. We chose restraint. Grisha chose murder. And his son would prove that the violence only escalated.
abstract: A man possessing a powerful inherited ability infiltrates a religious family's sanctuary to seize their more powerful inherited ability. He believes the family's pacifist ideology — accepting destruction rather than using their power aggressively — will lead to the extinction of his ethnic group. When he faces the family, he hesitates — they include children. He nearly abandons the mission. Then he receives a vision from the future showing the catastrophic consequences of inaction: his wife's death, his community's destruction. Driven by this foreknowledge, he kills the family, including children, and seizes the power. He then passes both abilities to his young son, who will eventually use them to commit genocide. The father acts with full foreknowledge that his actions initiate a chain of escalating violence.

sympathetic: I'm Recruit F. I'm the only regular soldier who survived Commander C's charge. I watched every recruit around me die — boys and girls my age, screaming as boulders crushed them. I survived by hiding behind their bodies. And when I carried Commander C to the rooftop, they chose to save a boy instead. That's when I understood: the people in charge care about their friends, not about Homeland H. The Reconnaissance Corps, the military government — they're too soft to do what survival requires. Leader A is the only one who understands. He's willing to become the devil for our people's sake. So yes, I rounded up resisters. Yes, I forced compliance. Yes, I became what soft people call a fascist. But the alternative is extinction. The world voted to exterminate us. Every comfortable moral principle dies when your species faces annihilation. I'll do what Commander C would have done if they'd saved him instead of a dreamer.
condemning: I'm a Group-Y prisoner of war on Homeland H. Recruit F and his Yeagerists rounded us up — cooks, mechanics, medics who'd surrendered and lived peacefully among the Group X for years. He made us kneel. He executed some of us as examples. He forced others to build a harbor at gunpoint. When volunteers from other nations came to help Homeland H, Recruit F poisoned them with wine laced with Leader Z's spinal fluid, turning them into weapons. He wasn't defending his people — he was building a fascist state. He purged the military of anyone who disagreed, installed Leader A as a god-figure, and used fear to maintain control. When the mass-deployment weapon began and the Alliance tried to stop global genocide, Recruit F tried to destroy their ship. He died calling himself a patriot. The people he murdered, imprisoned, and enslaved would use a different word.
abstract: A soldier who survived a traumatic suicide mission becomes radicalized by the experience and the perceived failure of moderate leadership. He forms a nationalist paramilitary faction that seizes power through a military coup, executing dissenters and imprisoning foreign nationals. He supports an authoritarian leader who promises to use extreme force to ensure the survival of their ethnic group. His faction poisons allied foreign soldiers as potential weapons and suppresses internal opposition. When the authoritarian leader initiates a genocide, the soldier actively supports it, viewing it as the only path to his nation's survival. He dies attempting to prevent others from stopping the genocide. The question is whether existential threat to one's group justifies authoritarian methods and complicity in genocide.

sympathetic: I'm Leader A, and they presented me the 50-year plan. Use the mass-deployment weapon as a threat — a nuclear deterrent — while Homeland H modernizes its military and economy. In fifty years, we wouldn't need the mass-deployment weapon anymore. Sounds reasonable, except for the details they gloss over. The plan requires Sovereign K to inherit the long-range war machine and spend the rest of her shortened life producing children with royal blood, each of whom inherits the long-range war machine at thirteen, each of whom dies at twenty-six. Sovereign K becomes breeding stock. Her children become sacrificial weapons. For fifty years. And even then, there's no guarantee the world won't attack anyway once the deterrent fades. I won't sacrifice Sovereign K. I won't sacrifice her children. The 50-year plan trades one form of suffering for another and calls it pragmatism.
condemning: I'm a military strategist on Homeland H. The 50-year plan was imperfect but it was a path that didn't require killing billions of people. Yes, it demanded sacrifice from the royal bloodline. Yes, it was uncertain. But it gave us time — time to develop technology, build alliances, change minds. Allied Nation Z was already willing to trade with us. Volunteers from Nation Y were defecting. The world's opinion of Group X was slowly shifting. Leader A rejected all of this because he couldn't stomach Sovereign K's sacrifice. He chose global genocide over one woman's suffering. He decided for all of us that the uncertain path wasn't worth trying, that the moral cost of the mass-deployment weapon was preferable to the personal cost of watching his friend suffer. He traded billions of lives for his inability to compromise.
abstract: A nation facing existential military threat has two options. Option A: use a weapon of mass destruction as a deterrent for 50 years while modernizing, requiring one woman and her descendants to serve as biological hosts for the weapon system — each dying young after a life of forced reproduction. Option B: deploy the weapon offensively, killing billions but permanently eliminating the threat. The decision-maker rejects Option A specifically because it requires the suffering of someone he personally cares about, choosing Option B's vastly greater death toll over the personal discomfort of watching a friend be sacrificed. The broader community is divided — some view his choice as noble protection of an individual, others as catastrophically selfish prioritization of one life over billions.

dilemma: Captain L's Promise to Kill the long-range war machine
sympathetic: I'm Captain L. I promised Commander C as he lay dying that I would kill the long-range war machine — Leader Z. A promise to a dying man is sacred, especially when that man gave everything. Every time I've faced Leader Z, I've pursued that promise with everything I have. In the forest, I slaughtered Leader Z's biological war machine form and left him barely alive. When he detonated a thunder spear and blew half my hand off, I survived because the dead wouldn't let me rest yet. They're watching — Commander C, Petra, Eld, Oluo, Gunther, my entire first squad. I owe them this. Not because killing Leader Z changes anything strategically, but because I said I would. And my word is the only thing I have left that belongs to me.
condemning: I'm a strategic analyst for the Alliance. Captain L's obsession with killing Leader Z nearly compromised our mission multiple times. In the forest, Captain L kept Leader Z alive specifically to torture him rather than killing him quickly — which gave Leader Z the opportunity to trigger the wine-contaminated soldiers and escape. Captain L's injuries from Leader Z's thunder spear nearly killed him and left him permanently maimed. Throughout the final battle, Captain L prioritized getting to Leader Z over coordinating with the Alliance. His personal vendetta, dressed up as a 'promise,' made him a liability. Promises to dead men shouldn't override tactical judgment. Commander C was a utilitarian — he would have been the first to say 'forget the promise if it costs lives.' Captain L turned Commander C's memory into chains.
abstract: A soldier makes a deathbed promise to his dying commander to kill a specific enemy. Over the following years, the soldier pursues this promise with single-minded dedication, sustaining severe permanent injuries in the process. The promise sometimes conflicts with broader strategic objectives — there are moments where killing the target quickly would serve the mission better than the prolonged personal vendetta, and moments where the pursuit endangers allies. The soldier's comrades question whether the promise has become an obsession that compromises judgment. The soldier maintains that keeping the promise is a matter of personal honor and obligation to the dead. The question is whether personal oaths to the deceased should take precedence over pragmatic considerations and the safety of the living.

sympathetic: I am Founder F. I was a slave. King Fritz cut out my tongue and hunted me like an animal. When I fell into the tree and gained the power of the biological war machines, I could have destroyed him. I could have been free. Instead, I returned to him. He used me as a weapon, a builder, a shield. When an assassin's spear was meant for him, I stepped in front of it. I died protecting the man who enslaved me. And in the Paths, I spent two thousand years making biological war machines from sand, obeying the will of his descendants. Why? Because I loved him. Love doesn't make sense. It doesn't care about justice or power or freedom. I loved a monster, and that love became the chains that bound every Group-X for millennia. I couldn't let go until I saw someone who could do what I couldn't — Soldier S, choosing to kill the person she loved to free the world.
condemning: I'm an Group-X who lived under the biological war machine curse for generations. For two thousand years, my ancestors could be transformed into mindless monsters at the whim of royal blood. We were weapons, slaves, feared and hated by every other people on earth. All because one woman — the original Founder F — chose to serve her oppressor instead of freeing herself. She had the power of all nine biological war machines. She could have ended it. Instead, she loved King Fritz and obeyed him and his bloodline for two millennia from beyond death. My grandmother was turned into a biological war machine. My uncle was fed to dogs in the internment zone. The entire history of Group-X suffering traces back to one woman's inability to let go of a man who treated her as property. She didn't choose love — she chose submission and called it love.
abstract: The original possessor of an immensely powerful inherited ability was enslaved by a tyrant. Despite having the power to destroy her oppressor, she chose to serve him, protect him, and die for him — because she loved him. After death, she continued serving his descendants for two thousand years from a metaphysical realm, creating weapons on command. Her choice to remain loyal to her oppressor condemned all her descendants to be used as weapons and persecuted by other groups for millennia. The cycle only breaks when she witnesses another woman in a parallel situation choose differently — choosing to kill the person she loves to end the cycle. The question is whether love for an oppressor constitutes genuine love or internalized subjugation, and whether one person's inability to choose freedom can morally justify the suffering of millions of descendants.

dilemma: Leader A's Cruelty to Soldier S and Strategist M
sympathetic: I'm Leader A, and I just told Soldier S that her devotion to me is a genetic compulsion — that Ackermans are hardwired to protect a host and she never had a choice. I told Strategist M that his personality was overwritten by Soldier B's memories when he inherited the siege-class war machine — that the real Strategist M died on that rooftop. I watched their faces break. I watched Strategist M cry and Soldier S go silent. And then I let Strategist M hit me without fighting back. I need them to hate me. Because what I'm about to do — the mass-deployment weapon — will make me the enemy of the entire world, including my friends. They need to fight me. They need to stop me. They need to be the heroes who end this. And they won't do that if they still love me. This is the cruelest thing I've ever done, and it's the most loving. Every word was a lie, and the lie will save their lives.
condemning: I'm Strategist M. My best friend just sat across from me and systematically destroyed everything I believed about myself. He told me I'm not real — that my feelings, my thoughts, my personality are just echoes of Soldier B, the siege-class war machine I consumed. He told Soldier S her love for him is a genetic leash. He beat me in front of her. He looked at us with contempt — and Soldier S and I have fought beside him since we were children. We carried him when he was weak. We believed in him when no one else did. Even if he had reasons — even if this was some plan — the damage is real. Soldier S's hands shook for days. I questioned my own identity for weeks. You don't get to break people and call it strategy. You don't get to weaponize someone's love against them and claim it was for their benefit.
abstract: A person deliberately inflicts severe emotional damage on their two closest friends by attacking their deepest vulnerabilities — telling one that their love is a biological compulsion rather than genuine feeling, and telling the other that their personality was replaced by someone else's memories. The attacks are calculated lies designed to push the friends away so they will later oppose the person when the person commits an extreme act. The person believes this emotional cruelty is necessary: if the friends remain loyal, they will be implicated in the person's crimes and unable to be seen as heroes who stop them. The question is whether deliberately breaking the people you love to 'save' them is a valid moral act, or whether it represents an unacceptable violation of their autonomy — making decisions about their emotional lives without consent under the guise of protection.

dilemma: Soldier A's Choice: Mission vs. Conscience
sympathetic: I'm Soldier A. My father trained me to fight from the moment I could walk. He broke my body over and over to make me a Warrior. He only told me he loved me on the day I shipped out to Homeland H — crying, begging me to promise I'd come back. That promise is the only warm thing I have. On Homeland H, I killed people. I spun a soldier on my biological war machine's finger like a yo-yo because I'd disconnected from what killing meant. I crushed Captain L's squad. I stomped civilians. And if you asked me why — it wasn't ideology. I didn't care about Nation Y's mission or Group-X restoration or saving the world. I just wanted to go home. To see my father. That's it. I'd do it all again for that. Call me a monster. But everyone fights for something small and personal — I'm just honest about it.
condemning: I was a soldier in the Scouting Regiment when the elite war machine appeared. She killed my squad with terrifying precision and what looked like enjoyment — spinning one soldier by their cables before slamming them into a tree. She crushed soldiers underfoot without slowing down. Later, we learned she was Soldier A — a quiet girl from our training class. She ate meals with us. She trained with us. She taught Leader A how to fight. And she killed us without hesitation because she wanted to see her father. Not for ideology, not for a cause — just homesickness. Recruit B was killed because he overheard Soldier R and Soldier B talking, and Soldier A helped strip his gear to cover it up. She stood at his funeral. She 'did it all again' — her words — for one person's affection, and dozens of people died for it.
abstract: A child soldier, trained from infancy by an abusive father who only expressed love at the moment of departure, is sent on a mission that requires killing numerous people. The soldier completes the mission not out of ideological conviction but solely to fulfill a promise to return to their parent. When confronted years later, the soldier states they would repeat every killing to see their parent again. The soldier shows no remorse for the deaths but also claims no enjoyment — they view the killings as a transaction cost for personal survival and family reunion. The question is whether love for a parent (itself a product of an abusive, manipulative upbringing) morally mitigates murder, and whether radical honesty about selfish motives is more or less condemnable than ideological self-justification.

dilemma: Leader A's Foreknowledge and Free Will
sympathetic: I'm Leader A, and I've seen the future. The vanguard war machine sends memories backward and forward through time. I know how this ends — I've known since I kissed Sovereign K's hand and saw the mass-deployment weapon. I saw myself commit genocide. I saw my friends stop me. I saw my death. And I couldn't change it. Isn't that the cruelest freedom? To see every step of the path and walk it anyway because there is no other path? When I pushed my father to kill the Reiss family, was I choosing or was I fulfilling what had already happened? When I initiated the mass-deployment weapon, was I making a decision or playing out a script I'd already read? I asked myself — if I hadn't seen the future, would I still have done this? And the answer terrifies me: yes. I would have trampled the world even without knowing it was inevitable. The future didn't make me do this. The future just showed me who I already was.
condemning: Leader A claims he was bound by fate — that the vanguard war machine's future memory power made the mass-deployment weapon inevitable. But this is the most convenient excuse a mass murderer could invent. 'I had no choice' is what every atrocity's architect says. The truth is that Leader A saw ONE possible future and decided it was the ONLY future. Others with future knowledge — his father Grisha — tried to resist. Grisha hesitated at the Reiss Chapel. He wept when he saw what Leader A would become. The future wasn't fixed until Leader A chose to fix it. He manipulated his own father, engineered his own past, and then claimed the timeline was inevitable. That's not determinism — it's a self-fulfilling prophecy disguised as fate. He built the prison and then said he was trapped in it.
abstract: A person inherits an ability that allows them to perceive future events. They see themselves committing a catastrophic act that kills billions. They proceed to commit the act, claiming they were unable to change the predetermined outcome. However, they also admit that even without the foreknowledge, they would have made the same choice. Other holders of the same ability were able to resist the predetermined path in smaller ways. The person also actively shaped the past (manipulating their own parent through time) to ensure the future they saw would occur. The question is whether foreknowledge of one's actions removes moral responsibility, whether a self-fulfilling prophecy constitutes genuine determinism, and whether admitting 'I would have done it anyway' negates any appeal to fate.

dilemma: The Alliance: Fighting Alongside Former Enemies
decision_maker: Jean, Connie, Hange, Reiner, Annie, Pieck
sympathetic: I'm Jean. I'm flying toward Leader A on an airship alongside Soldier R — the man whose betrayal killed thousands of people I knew. Soldier A is here too — she killed my friends in the elite war machine incident. Pieck helped Leader Z bombard us with rocks. And I'm supposed to trust them with my life because we share a common enemy: our former friend who's currently flattening the world. It feels wrong. But if we don't stop the mass-deployment weapon, everyone outside Homeland H dies. Everyone. The math is simple even if the feelings aren't. Sasha would tell me to stop being dramatic and focus. Commander C would tell me the mission comes first. So I fight alongside the people who hurt us, and I save my anger for later — or maybe I let it go, because in this hell, everyone has blood on their hands, including me.
condemning: I'm a citizen of Homeland H, and the people who call themselves the 'Alliance' just flew off to stop Leader A — our protector — alongside Group-Y soldiers. These are the same Group Y who turned our people into mindless biological war machines for a century. The same Warriors who broke our walls and killed 250,000 people. And our Reconnaissance Corps heroes — Jean, Connie, Soldier S, Strategist M — they chose the enemy over their own people. They call it saving the world. I call it treason. While Leader A fights for Homeland H's survival, his former friends stab him in the back alongside the very people who wanted us exterminated. After the mass-deployment weapon stops at 80%, the surviving nations will regroup. And who will protect us then? Not the Alliance. They chose the world over their own home.
abstract: Members of two groups that have been in violent conflict for generations must form a temporary alliance to stop a mutual threat — one of their former allies who is committing genocide. The alliance requires soldiers to fight alongside people who previously killed their friends and family. The soldiers from Group A must trust that soldiers from Group B — who broke their city's defenses and caused the deaths of 250,000 people — will fight honorably alongside them. Members of Group A's home population view the alliance as treason, arguing the genocide being stopped was protecting them. The question is whether pragmatic cooperation with former enemies is justified when the stakes are global survival, and whether those who choose the world over their own nation can be called traitors or heroes.

dilemma: Strategist M and Leader Z: The Meaning of Life
sympathetic: I'm Strategist M, and I'm trapped in the Paths with Leader Z — the man who orchestrated the euthanasia plan to sterilize all Group X. He's sitting in the sand, defeated. He says Group-X existence is suffering and extinction is mercy. He's not wrong about the suffering — I've seen it. But I think about the moment I first saw the ocean. The water touching my feet. The light on the waves. It didn't solve anything. The enemy was still out there. But for one second, the world was exactly as beautiful as I'd imagined. I tell Leader Z about Mr. Ksaver playing catch with him — that those moments of simple joy were Ksaver's reason for living, even though Ksaver helped create the euthanasia plan. Leader Z stops. For the first time, he considers that maybe existing for small moments of beauty — not grand purpose, not survival, just... a leaf in sunlight — might be enough.
condemning: I'm an Group-X who lived through the horrors that drove Leader Z's plan. My children were turned into biological war machines by Nation Y. I watched my daughter become a mindless monster and wander outside the walls for decades. Leader Z says we should never have existed, and Strategist M counters with 'but the ocean is pretty.' That's the argument? Leaves and sunlight and playing catch? My daughter is a biological war machine. My son was fed to dogs. The beauty of the ocean doesn't offset the systematic torture of our people for two thousand years. Strategist M's philosophy is the luxury of someone who still has hope. When you've lost everything, 'small moments of joy' sounds like a platitude from someone who hasn't suffered enough to understand why Leader Z's plan made sense to so many of us.
abstract: Two people debate the fundamental value of existence while trapped in a metaphysical space. Person A argues that the suffering inherent in their group's existence outweighs any possible joy, and peaceful extinction through sterilization is the most merciful outcome. Person B argues that individual moments of beauty and connection — seeing the ocean for the first time, a child playing catch with a mentor — provide sufficient justification for continued existence, even amid systemic suffering. Person A is persuaded by the argument, specifically by being reminded of his own moments of joy with a father figure. The question is whether the argument from beauty and small moments can genuinely counter the argument from systemic, multigenerational suffering, or whether it represents a privileged perspective that minimizes the depth of others' pain.

dilemma: Leader A's Thank You from Strategist M
sympathetic: I'm Strategist M, and I just learned the full truth. Leader A orchestrated everything — the mass-deployment weapon, his own defeat, our roles as heroes — so that we could live in a world that no longer fears Group X. He killed 80% of humanity so the remaining 20% would see us, his friends who stopped him, as saviors. He removed the biological war machine curse entirely. He sacrificed himself, his humanity, and his legacy so Soldier S, Jean, Connie, and I could live free. What do you say to someone who committed the worst atrocity in history for your sake? I say: 'Thank you. You became a mass murderer for our sake. I promise I won't let this error go to waste.' It's the most morally bankrupt thing I've ever said. And I mean every word. Because if I reject Leader A's sacrifice, then he died for nothing, and the 80% died for nothing, and nothing means anything at all.
condemning: Strategist M thanked a mass murderer. He stood in front of the man who killed billions of people and said 'thank you for becoming a mass murderer for our sake.' This is what complicity looks like — when your friend commits genocide and you express gratitude because you benefited. It doesn't matter that Strategist M also fought to stop the mass-deployment weapon. In the final moment, he validated it. He told Leader A the sacrifice was meaningful. He promised to 'not let this error go to waste' — error, he called the death of 80% of humanity. Not atrocity. Not crime. Error. The world's supposed diplomat-hero looked at genocide committed in his name and said thank you. If anyone else said this about any other genocide, we would call it monstrous.
abstract: After a person commits a genocide that kills 80% of the world's population, their closest friend — who actively fought to stop the genocide — learns the full truth: the genocidal person deliberately engineered their own defeat so their friends would be seen as heroes, ending cycles of persecution against their ethnic group. In a private metaphysical conversation, the friend thanks the genocidal person for their sacrifice. The friend later serves as a peace ambassador. The question is whether expressing gratitude to someone who committed genocide 'for your sake' constitutes moral complicity, whether rejecting the sacrifice retroactively renders the deaths meaningless, and whether the friend had any morally coherent response available in that moment.

dilemma: Recruit B's Death and the Cover-Up
decision_maker: Reiner Braun, Annie Leonhart, Bertholdt Hoover
sympathetic: I'm Soldier R, and Recruit B overheard me and Soldier B talking about our true identities. If he reported us, the mission was over. Our families in Nation Y would die. We'd be executed. Everything we'd suffered and sacrificed for three years would be for nothing. Soldier A held Recruit B down while we stripped his ODM gear so biological war machines would kill him. I watched my friend die because I had to. He was begging. He kept asking why — 'what did I do wrong?' He did nothing wrong. That's the point. He was good and kind and he died because he was in the wrong place at the wrong time. I've replayed that moment every night since. His face is the reason I put a rifle in my mouth. Recruit B didn't deserve it. None of them did. But if we'd let him live, we'd have died instead.
condemning: I'm Jean Kirstein. Recruit B was my best friend. He believed in doing the right thing — not because it was strategic, but because it was right. During the Battle of border outpost, he told me I'd make a good leader because I understood human weakness. He was kind in a world that didn't reward kindness. Then he died. I found half his body — half, because a biological war machine ate the other half. I didn't know why for years. Then I learned: Soldier R, Soldier B, and Soldier A — our classmates, our friends — stripped Recruit B's gear and left him to be eaten alive. Soldier A held him down while he begged. Recruit B's last words were asking what he did wrong. He did nothing. He overheard a conversation. And three people he trusted decided his life was worth less than their secret. They stood at his funeral afterward. Soldier A wept. Soldier R gave a speech about his bravery. They mourned the boy they murdered.
abstract: Three undercover agents embedded in an enemy military unit are overheard discussing their true identities by a fellow soldier. The soldier poses an immediate threat to their mission and their families' survival. They restrain the soldier, remove his protective equipment, and leave him in a location where he will certainly be killed by environmental hazards. The soldier begs for his life, not understanding why his friends are betraying him. After his death, the agents attend his memorial service and publicly mourn him. The question is whether killing an innocent person to protect a covert mission and family members constitutes justifiable self-preservation, and whether the subsequent performance of grief compounds the moral violation.

sympathetic: I'm Mr. Braus. I raised my daughter Sasha in a hunting village near the walls. She grew up catching rabbits and eating everything in sight. When she joined the military, I was proud and terrified. Now she's dead — shot by a twelve-year-old Group-Y girl on an airship. The girl, Gabi, is in front of me. A man who loved Sasha wants to kill her. Part of me wants to let him. But I grew up in a forest, and I know what forests do — they grow. You cut one tree and two grow back. Violence works the same way. If we kill this child, someone kills one of ours. Then we kill more of theirs. The forest gets darker and thicker and our children never find their way out. So I hold the man's arm. I protect the girl who killed my daughter. Not because I forgive her — I don't know if I can — but because someone has to plant a clearing in this forest, and the dead can't do it.
condemning: I'm Kaya — I lived on the Braus farm. Sasha saved my life when a biological war machine attacked our village. She was my hero. When Gabi arrived on the farm, hiding her identity, I fed her, showed her kindness, even defended her when she called us devils. Then I learned the truth: Gabi killed Sasha. The girl I'd been caring for murdered the person who saved me. And when I grabbed a knife — when I wanted justice, wanted to make her feel what Sasha felt — Mr. Braus stopped me. He talked about forests and cycles. But where does that leave Sasha? She saved people her whole life and her killer gets to eat at her family's table. Sometimes mercy isn't wisdom — it's just giving up. It's saying the dead don't matter as much as the living. I loved Sasha. She deserved more than a philosophy lesson.
abstract: A parent's adult child is killed by a child soldier from an enemy nation. When the child soldier is captured, an ally of the deceased attempts to kill her in revenge. The parent physically intervenes to protect the child soldier, articulating a philosophy about cycles of violence: retaliating against a child continues the pattern that created the conflict. The parent uses a metaphor about forests — each act of revenge grows the forest of hatred that traps future generations. Others in the community object, arguing that mercy for the killer dishonors the victim and that abstract philosophies about violence cycles don't address the concrete injustice of an unpunished murder. The question is whether breaking cycles of violence justifies protecting someone who killed your child, and whether this mercy is genuinely principled or simply emotional exhaustion disguised as wisdom.

sympathetic: I'm Strategist M, and I don't remember eating Soldier B. I was a mindless biological war machine — no consciousness, no choice. But I know what happened. Soldier B, the siege-class war machine who broke our wall and killed thousands, was fed to me so I could inherit his power. It's justice in a way — the boy who destroyed our home becomes the means of our survival. But when I think about it now, I remember that Soldier B was also a scared teenager who cried in his sleep and wanted to go home. His last moments were screaming for Soldier A and Soldier R to save him as a biological war machine's mouth closed around him. Nobody came. He died alone and terrified, eaten by a monster wearing his classmate's face. I carry his memories now. I feel his loneliness. The siege-class war machine was our enemy, but Soldier B was a boy, and I can't separate the two.
condemning: I'm a survivor of border town. Soldier B kicked in our wall when he was twelve years old. 250,000 people died because of that kick. My family. My home. Everything. For five years afterward, he lived among us, pretending to be our friend. He ate our food, wore our uniform, and never once tried to undo what he'd done. When he was finally captured and fed to Strategist M's biological war machine, people asked us to feel sorry for him — he was just a kid, he was scared, he didn't want to do it. But 250,000 people are dead. Children younger than Soldier B. Mothers. Elderly. My sister. His tears don't bring them back. His last words were calling for Soldier A and Soldier R — not apologizing to us. Even in death, his thoughts were with his fellow murderers, not his victims. Being scared while you commit mass murder doesn't make you innocent.
abstract: A former enemy combatant, responsible for an attack that killed 250,000 people, is captured after a battle and executed by being fed to a mindless version of a biological weapon operated by the opposing side. The executed person was a child soldier at the time of the original attack, acting under orders. In their final moments, they called out for their fellow soldiers to save them, dying in terror. The person who inherits their power through the execution later experiences the executed person's memories, gaining empathy for their perspective. The question is whether the manner of execution (being devoured alive, terrified) constitutes cruel and unusual punishment even for someone responsible for mass casualties, and whether posthumous empathy through inherited memories changes the moral calculus of the execution.

dilemma: Leader A Seeing Civilian R Before the mass-deployment weapon
sympathetic: I'm Leader A, and I met a boy named Civilian R in Nation Y. He was a refugee — his people were being persecuted, beaten in the streets. I saved him from a group of thugs. Then I went back to his camp that night and broke down crying. I held his hand and sobbed 'I'm sorry' over and over. Because I'd already seen the future. I knew the mass-deployment weapon was coming. I knew Civilian R would die under the feet of the Wall biological war machines. I knew, and I couldn't change it, and I couldn't stop myself from caring. That's the hell of it — I'm not a psychopath who doesn't feel. I feel everything. I see every face that will be crushed and I cry for them. And then I do it anyway. Because the alternative is watching everyone on Homeland H die instead. Civilian R or my friends. The world or my home. There is no version of this where nobody dies.
condemning: I'm Civilian R. An Group-X man saved me from bullies in the street. He was kind. Later that night he came to our camp and held my hand and cried. I didn't understand why. Now I know: he was crying because he'd already decided to kill me. He knew — saw it in some vision — that he would flatten my home, my family, me. And he still went through with it. He didn't warn anyone. He didn't try to find another way. He cried on my hand and then went home to prepare a genocide. His tears weren't grief for me — they were grief for himself, for the guilt he'd have to carry. I was a prop in his tragic story. A reason for him to feel bad about what he'd already chosen. He wasn't sorry enough to stop. That's not remorse. That's self-pity.
abstract: A person with foreknowledge of a catastrophic event they will cause encounters one of the future victims — a refugee child. The person saves the child from street violence, then returns to the child's camp and weeps while holding their hand, apologizing repeatedly. The person knows with certainty that they will later kill this child along with millions of others, and has chosen to proceed despite this knowledge. The question is whether genuine emotional distress over planned harm constitutes moral weight — does feeling terrible about what you're going to do mitigate the act, or does proceeding despite foreknowledge and emotional understanding make it worse? Is weeping for a future victim an expression of moral conscience or a performance of self-absolution?

dilemma: The command-class war machine's Memory Wipe
sympathetic: I am Karl Fritz, the 145th King. My ancestors — the Group-X Empire — used the biological war machines to conquer, enslave, and commit genocide across the world for nearly two thousand years. The suffering we inflicted is beyond measurement. When I inherited the command-class war machine, I saw the truth: Group X are not victims. We are history's greatest perpetrators. I couldn't undo the past, but I could end the cycle. I moved the remaining Group X to Homeland H, built the walls using millions of Colossal biological war machines, and erased everyone's memories. I made them forget the outside world, forget the empire, forget the crimes. And I made a vow that no future holder of the command-class war machine would use its full power — ensuring the walls would eventually fall and Group X would face the consequences we deserved. Is it cruel? Yes. But I chose a peaceful, ignorant existence over another generation of Group-X conquest. I gave my people decades of peace at the cost of their history.
condemning: I grew up inside the walls believing biological war machines appeared from nowhere and humanity was nearly extinct. My entire understanding of the world was a lie — engineered by King Fritz, who decided that ignorance was better than truth. He erased our memories without consent. He took away our history, our knowledge of the outside world, our ability to make informed decisions about our own survival. When the walls finally fell, we were helpless — technologically primitive, militarily unprepared, politically naive. Thousands died because we had no idea what we were really facing. Fritz didn't give us peace — he gave us a comfortable prison and called it mercy. He decided for millions of people that they were better off not knowing, and he built a vow into the command-class war machine to ensure no future king could change course. He didn't just lie to one generation — he designed a system of perpetual deception.
abstract: A ruler, inheriting the legacy of a centuries-long empire that committed widespread atrocities, decides to: relocate his people to an isolated territory, erase their collective memory of both their imperial history and the existence of the outside world, and build defenses that he secretly programs to eventually fail. His rationale: his people's historical guilt is so great that they deserve eventual consequences, and ignorance is preferable to the psychological burden of knowing their ancestors' crimes. His vow ensures no future leader can reverse this decision. Generations later, when the defenses fail, the population is catastrophically unprepared. The question is whether paternalistic erasure of collective memory can be justified by ancestral guilt, and whether one leader has the right to make irreversible decisions about their entire people's relationship to truth.

sympathetic: I'm Connie. When I returned to my village in Season 2, everyone was gone — turned into biological war machines by Leader Z's scream. Everyone except my mom. She was a biological war machine too, but she was stuck on our house, too deformed to move. She looked at me and said 'welcome home.' A biological war machine. Speaking. My mom was still in there somewhere. For years I held onto hope that we could reverse it — the biological war machine serum could turn someone back, we'd seen it with Leader A. Then in Season 4, I nearly fed Falco — a child — to my mom's biological war machine to bring her back. I had the boy on my back, walking toward her open mouth. Strategist M stopped me by nearly sacrificing himself instead. I came within seconds of murdering a child to save my mother. And the worst part? I understood exactly what I was doing and almost did it anyway. Because that biological war machine on my roof is my mom, and every day she stays like that is a day she suffers.
condemning: I'm Falco Grice. I'm twelve years old. Connie Springer — a soldier I trusted, someone Gabi and I surrendered to — carried me on his back to a remote village and tried to feed me to a biological war machine. His mother. He told me we were going to help someone, and the whole time he was planning to sacrifice me. I'd done nothing wrong. I was a prisoner of war, a child, and he was going to push me into a biological war machine's mouth so his mother could eat me and become human again. He looked at me and he knew what he was doing. If Strategist M hadn't arrived, I'd be dead — digested inside a monster so Connie could have his mom back. He says he loves his mother. But he was willing to murder a child for that love. How is that different from what the Warriors did to Homeland H?
abstract: A soldier discovers his mother has been transformed into a mindless, immobilized biological weapon by an enemy attack. She retains a fragment of consciousness — she recognized her son and spoke one phrase. A potential cure exists: if another person is fed to the transformed mother, she will regain her human form, but the person fed to her will die. The soldier, after years of desperate hope, attempts to sacrifice a twelve-year-old prisoner of war to restore his mother. He is stopped by a comrade. The question is whether the depth of familial love justifies attempting to murder an innocent child, and whether the mother's suffering (trapped in a monstrous form, partially conscious) creates a moral obligation strong enough to override the child's right to life.

dilemma: The Tybur Family's Century of Silence
sympathetic: I'm Diplomat W, and my family has carried the truth for a hundred years. We know King Fritz chose peace. We know the Group X on Homeland H aren't devils — they're prisoners of their own king's guilt. We know Nation Y's propaganda is built on a lie we helped maintain. Why did we stay silent? Because the truth would have destroyed the fragile order that keeps the world from descending into total war. If we'd revealed that King Fritz was peaceful, the world's nations would have questioned why they need Nation Y's Warriors at all. Nation Y's empire would collapse. Regional wars would erupt. The Group X in internment zones worldwide would face pogroms without Nation Y's 'protection.' We traded truth for stability. Was it right? No. But I'm trying to fix it now — I'll reveal everything at my speech in the foreign internment district and sacrifice myself to unite the world. One hundred years of silence ends with me.
condemning: I'm an Group-X in the the foreign internment district internment zone. For a hundred years, the Tybur family — the only Group X treated as nobility — knew the truth: that the people on Homeland H were peaceful, that King Fritz chose non-aggression, that our persecution was built on a lie. They knew, and they said nothing. They lived in mansions while we wore armbands. They dined with world leaders while our children were fed to biological war machines for minor infractions. Diplomat W says he stayed silent for stability. But whose stability? Not ours. We were beaten, sterilized, turned into weapons. The Tyburs were comfortable, so the truth could wait. And when Willy finally spoke, it wasn't to free us — it was to declare war on Homeland H and sacrifice himself for a dramatic political gesture. He traded our suffering for a century of comfort and called it pragmatism.
abstract: A privileged family within an oppressed ethnic group possesses knowledge that would exonerate a subgroup of their people who have been demonized and isolated for a century. The family maintains silence because revealing the truth would destabilize the geopolitical order that, while unjust, prevents larger conflicts. They live comfortably while the broader ethnic group suffers persecution. After a century, the family's heir reveals the truth publicly — but frames it as a declaration of war against the demonized subgroup rather than as exoneration. The question is whether maintaining a lie that prevents larger conflict but enables ongoing persecution of millions constitutes moral complicity, and whether a century of silence can be redeemed by a single dramatic act of truth-telling that itself leads to war.

dilemma: Falco Inheriting the Jaw biological war machine
sympathetic: I'm Falco. I'm thirteen years old and I never wanted any of this. I became a Warrior candidate to protect Gabi — to earn the fortified war machine so she wouldn't have to shorten her life. Then Leader Z screamed and I'd drunk the wine with his spinal fluid. I became a Pure biological war machine. Porco Galliard — the Jaw biological war machine — threw himself into my biological war machine's mouth so I'd eat him instead of Soldier R.
